title: Perception: detectors for monsters, loot, events and the Lie Detector
tagline: Questions answered about one frame: monsters, drops, deaths, newborns, touches, messages, Lie Detector.
summary: These modules turn a frame of the game into answers: which monsters are where and which way they face, which drops lie on the platforms, which followed monster is dying, which spawn point has a monster fading in, whether a monster just touched her (MISS or damage), what the game's message bar and chat box show, and whether a Lie Detector test is on screen. They know nothing about the map: localization places their answers and behavior acts on them. Most run on every frame of the perception service's one pass (15 a second); the Lie Detector spotter runs in the elevated key player's watchdog, 4 times a second.
details_md:
Every detector here answers one question about pixels and returns frame pixels; `localization` (the `Scene`, `worldstate`, `tracking`) turns those into map units. They are called from three places:

- **The perception service's per-frame pass** (`localization.worldstate.WorldStep.step`, 15 frames a second, one pass reads everything off one frame): the whole-screen monster search (`MobDetector.detect_wide`, on the pass's one-thread pool 'wide' beside her look, followed on that thread by `perception.exact`'s finder, another slice, which adds the partly covered monsters near her that the masked search misses), the spawn watch (`SpawnWatch.look`), the death watch (`DeathWatch.dying` for tracks found weakly or lost lately), the touch watch (`TouchWatch.update`), the chat box (`chatbox.read`, in `Eyes.look_at`) and the drop strips a consumer asked for, then one strip in view by rotation every 0.2 s (worldstate's `DROPS_STRIPS`, `DROPS_EVERY_S`; `LootDetector.detect_each` through `Eyes.items_in`).
- **The hunt's own questions**, through `Eyes` (perception's door to pixels, another slice): her attack's MISS over her targets (`MissReader`), the message bar's refusals (`ChatReader`), the pickup log's rows (`log_rows`, `says_full`, `says_no_darts`).
- **The Lie Detector chain**: the elevated key player's watchdog (`control.player.Watchdog`) asks `LieDetectorSpotter` 4 times a second; once the alarm is up, the perception service runs `lie_target.TargetTracker` on the mouse mini-game (in a child process of its own, `control.lie_tracking`) and `violetta` on the Violetta game (on a thread of its own, `control.violetta_live`).

| Detector | Question | How | Cost (measured) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `MobDetector` | which monsters, where, facing | colour silhouettes, then masked picture match | a crowd's whole screen 14-17 ms on its thread, about 22 ms of CPU (2026-10-27) |
| `LootDetector` | which drops on a platform | masked shape match plus a colour check | her platform's strips 6-9 ms, every platform in view 54-111 ms |
| `DeathWatch` | is this track dying | die1 frames at its feet | 0.83 ms a look |
| `SpawnWatch` | is a monster fading in at a point | alpha-blend fit over the map's art | 1.19 ms a frame |
| `TouchWatch` | did a monster touch her | violet popup over her tag | 0.42 ms a frame |
| `MissReader` | did her attack miss | the orange MISS shape's IoU | about 0.12 ms a box |
| `ChatReader` | did the game refuse her key | pink line, OCR only when new | under 1 ms; 285 ms per new line |
| `chatbox.read` | is the chat box expanded | its +/- button and input row | 0.04-0.08 ms |
| `LieDetectorSpotter` | is a Lie Detector up | templates near each form's place | 11 ms near, 151 ms whole frame |
| `TargetTracker` | where is the mini-game's target | outline particle filter | 30 ms a frame |
| `violetta` | where did the made-up Violetta go | YOLO boxes plus the client's shuffle rules | about 10 ms a frame on the GPU |

**Shared techniques.**
- *The game's own pictures*: monster sprites, item icons and coins, die1 frames, the NoViolet and NoRed popup sprites, all read from the game data copy (`gamedata`) and drawn the way the look frame shows them. At the game's own 1366x768 (since 2026-10-23) a picture's opaque pixels appear exactly, so only alpha-255 pixels are matched: half-transparent ones are partly background.
- *Masked normalised correlation* (`perception.match`, in C where `gamelab.native` is built), and colour tests to reject look-alikes: hand-made palettes and learned gates in the monster search, `PIXEL_SLACK` for drops, HSV ranges for popups, the game's pink for its own lines.
- *Measured thresholds*: every number comes from labelled recordings, and the comments say which and where (scripts under D:/MapleHelper-scratch).
- *C hot paths with the same answers* as the numpy reference (`search.c`, `spawns.c`, `native.c`), which also release Python's lock so thread pools help.
- *False positives avoided before misses*: the spawn watch's rule has its nearest negative 11.8 times off it, and the spawn and death watches run only on the maps and kinds that were measured.

**Geometry.** Look frames are 1 px a game px at the game's own 1366x768; the older 1920x1080 window gave half-size look frames at 0.703 px a game px, where many numbers were first measured. Detectors take a `scale` (`Geometry.frame_scale`) or bring their pictures to it, and the Lie Detector templates (cut at 1920x1080) have frames stretched up to them.

**Safety.** `LieDetectorSpotter` is loaded by the elevated key player and imports only `gamelab.paths`. The mini-game tracker and the Violetta solver only say where; any cursor move or click goes through the elevated player, which refuses any that isn't inside the board or a button's box (`control.player`'s `alarm_refusal`, the boxes in `control.alarm`).

modules.title: Monster detector (MobDetector)
modules.tagline: Finds every monster on screen: colour silhouettes first, then masked picture matches.
modules.summary: MobDetector finds monsters in a look frame in two steps: a fast single-channel match of each picture's body-colour silhouette against the frame's body-colour mask, then a full masked colour match of the game's own picture at the best few spots. Each monster found is a `Mob` that knows its kind, which picture matched, where its feet are, which way it faces and its pose. The perception service's pass calls `detect_wide` over the whole play area on every frame (15 a second); its answers feed the monster tracker.
modules.details_md:
**The pictures.** Templates are PNGs named `<kind>_<anything>.png` (RGBA, the alpha is the mask): screenshot cut-outs in `gamelab/assets/mobs` and the game's own sprites that `perception.sprites` builds from the game data (every stand, move and hit1 frame). Each folder's `index.json` / `cutouts.json` says, per picture, where the monster's feet are (`origin`), which way it faces, its game frame (`move/2`) and body box; `scale.json` says its px per game px. Every picture is also used flipped (the game's sprites face left). At the game's own 1366x768 step 2 matches only the fully opaque pixels (alpha 255): a slime is see-through, and its half-opaque pixels on screen are partly what's behind it.

**Step 1: where to look.** The frame (or a band of rows) is shrunk to `SEARCH_SCALE` (the old 1920x1080 window's half size, 0.703 px per game px, where every step-1 number was measured) and then to 1/`COARSE`. Each kind's body-colour test makes a mask: hand-written for the first map's four kinds (`PALETTES`: pig, slime, snail, orange-mushroom), or a gate learned from the map's background colours (`perception.gates`) for every other kind. A kind is skipped where fewer than `MIN_BODY_PIXELS` have its colour. Each picture's silhouette is matched against the mask (`TM_CCOEFF_NORMED`); windows whose share of body colour is under `MIN_COVER` (0.25) times the silhouette's own share are zeroed first (their normalised score is noise that can reach 1.0), and 3x3 local peaks at `SILHOUETTE_THRESHOLD` (0.35) or more become spots.

**Step 2: is it really one.** At half size the best `MAX_CHECKS` (12) spots per kind, at least `CHECK_SLACK` apart, get the full masked colour match a few px around (a learned kind's place: its best `PER_PLACE`, 3, pictures); `THRESHOLD` (0.6) or more is a monster. On a finer frame (1366x768 at full size, the live case) spots are grouped into places; a place must first pass a gate at step 1's scale (`FINE_GATE` 0.55, trying `GATE_TRIES` pictures for learned kinds), then its best `FINE_TEMPLATES` (6) pictures are matched at full size within `FINE_SLACK` (4) px, because a monster's animation frames differ crisply there. Overlapping finds are suppressed (`match.suppress_overlaps`).

**Kinds that share a body.** Horny and Green Mushroom (one sprite, two caps) and Stump and Dark Stump (one sprite, two colours) have `SAME_SHAPE` (0.9) of their pixels in common: they are searched as one unit with one silhouette, and each kind's picture is checked side by side at a place. An Axe Stump is a Stump plus an axe (`TWIN_COVER` 0.8): a find is re-judged at its feet (`_pick_kind`), where a picture with parts of its own (`OWN_PARTS`, the axe) wins only if those parts alone match `OWN_MATCH` (0.6).

**The whole screen.** `detect_wide` cuts the play area into bands of `WIDE_BAND` rows every `WIDE_STEP`, overlapping by the tallest learned picture, each band getting its own best spots (one pass over the whole screen once lost three slimes to green foliage that took all the slime spots). Bands run at once on a thread pool.

**C, with the same answers.** Step 1 runs in `gamelab/search.c` (`_InC`, switch `SEARCH_C`) with exact integer sums; where OpenCV's float32 noise (bounded by `NOISE_K`) could change which windows peak or their order, those shapes are redone the OpenCV way (`_InC._master`), so the answers are the reference implementation's by construction. Step 2's matches go to `native.c`'s re-find contexts (`_matches`). Without the DLL everything runs in numpy and OpenCV with the same answers.

**Re-finds.** `refind`, `refind_all` and `refind_ahead` look for a followed monster near where it should be (`REFIND_PAD` 16 px, a smaller near window first, a memo of identical pixels, the animation's likely next frames, optionally on the GPU). Since 2026-10-30 the live pass searches the whole screen every frame instead and these are unused there, kept for analysis and tests.

**What it misses.** A monster partly covered near her (her body, her pet, damage numbers, effects) loses masked score with the share still showing: on a clip of 2026-11-02 it was found on 6% of the frames within 25 units of her, most misses refused at `FINE_GATE`. Since 2026-11-04 `perception.exact`'s finder (exact pixels of the same pictures, another slice) runs right after the search on the same thread and adds them.

modules.concurrency: Two lazily used ThreadPoolExecutors: 'monster-search' with THREADS (6) workers for the numpy/OpenCV path, and 'monster-search-bands' with min(threads, SEARCH_THREADS=3) for the whole screen's bands when step 1 is in C; each worker sets OpenCV to one thread. The C calls (search.c, native.c) release Python's GIL. Per-thread C re-find contexts (threading.local); locks guard lazy C setup and the counters. In the live pass the whole screen runs on worldstate's one-thread pool named 'wide' (`WorldStep._halves`, switch `HALVES`) beside her look.

decisions.what: Learned kinds' places gated with their first GATE_TRIES (2) pictures, not one.
decisions.why: A stump's flinch frame's silhouette matched best but scored 0.29-0.46 at the gate; with two tries 56 of 58 stumps in plain view were found instead of 53 (106 ms a whole screen against 91).

decisions.what: Kinds without a hand-made colour test get a gate learned from the map's background.
decisions.why: West Rocky Mountain II's stumps are browns like its rock and Tree Dungeon's mushrooms stand in a green forest: hand-written tests would be hard to write (README, learned gates).

decisions.what: Re-finds look in a near window first and recall a window's last answer when its pixels are identical.
decisions.why: Fewer matches a frame with the reference implementation's answers (README, Fewer re-find matches).

decisions.what: Step 1 moved into C (gamelab/search.c) with exact integer sums.
decisions.why: A crowd's whole screen took 115 ms of CPU on one thread, about 22 after (README, A cheaper whole screen).

decisions.what: OpenCV's float32 noise bound NOISE_K measured; shapes it could decide are redone the OpenCV way.
decisions.why: So the C search's answers equal the reference implementation's by construction, not only on the frames compared.

decisions.what: The live pass searches the whole screen every frame at 15 a second; re-finds left unused.
decisions.why: The user: "make perception output the 15fps whole screen only, no need for a separate 30fps existing tracking".

gotchas: A Mob's x and y are the picture's centre, not where it stands: use `foot_x` / `feet_y` (a sprite stands on its origin, up to 8.5 map units off its centre; a slime's hop frame ends 10 units above its feet).
Step 1's frame is cut to a multiple of COARSE: an odd band height (151 rows) once smeared faint colour into blank windows that then scored a perfect 1.0.
Kinds with neither a hand-made colour test nor the map's background counts aren't looked for at all; a detector given `kinds` may legitimately find nothing.
`_one_opencv_thread` sets OpenCV's thread count for the whole process, not just the pool's thread.
The re-find API (refind, refind_all, refind_ahead, native.c's rf_* and the GPU path) is unused by the live pass since 2026-10-30 and left for a later cleanup.
The search stops at the HUD's top (row 700 at 1366x768): a monster half under the chat bar, its feet below that row, isn't looked for.
Partly covered monsters near her are mostly missed (6% found within 25 units of her on a 2026-11-02 clip): perception.exact's finder, run after the search, adds them.

modules.title: Loot detector (LootDetector)
modules.tagline: Finds drops and mesos lying in strips just above the platforms.
modules.summary: LootDetector matches the game's own item pictures, and the spinning meso coins, in strips just above the platforms in view. A spot is a drop when the masked shape match scores 0.6 and its pixels are within 24 colour levels of the picture's, which rules out backdrops and UI that only share a shape. It also holds the pickup log's two text tests: inventory full (`says_full`) and no throwing stars left (`says_no_darts`).
modules.details_md:
**The pictures.** `build` draws each item's `iconRaw` from the game data copy (`gamedata.canvas.item_icon`; ids looked up by name in String/Etc.img and Consume.img, because Classic World's ids differ from GMS's) and the bronze and gold coins' spinning frames (the edge-on frame left out). They are drawn at the old 1920x1080 window's 1.40625 px per game px (`gamedata/data/out/loot`) or as they are for the game's own 1366x768 (`loot_x1`, with a `scale.json`). Shrinking averages colour over opaque pixels only (`resample_opaque`), so transparent pixels don't bleed into the edges. Each file is written under a temporary name and renamed (`_put`): the folder is shared by every map, and test workers may build it at once. `ensure` builds only what's missing.

**Matching** (`detect_each`). Callers pass boxes: `localization.scene.find_loot` asks for strips just above each platform (`ABOVE` 30 to `BELOW` 6 half-size px), since drops lie on the ground (a whole-screen search took 1.3 s). Every template is matched in every box at once on a 3-thread pool. Per template: masked `TM_CCOEFF_NORMED` (`match.masked_match`), local maxima in 5x5 at `THRESHOLD` (0.6), then the colour check: the mean absolute difference over the template's solid pixels (covering at least `SOLID_COVER` of a pixel) must be `PIXEL_SLACK` (24) or less. Measured: real drops 12-19 off, scenery and UI that matched a shape 27-57 off. Cost: 6.0 ms for her platform's strips and 54 for every platform in view (README, medians on 30 saved screenshots); with 3 threads on 100 frames of 2026-10-26, 8.6 and 111 ms. At the game's own size the pictures are drawn pixel for pixel, so the shape is matched on grey (one channel, faster), and colours are still checked.

**Recoloured twins.** Ores, gems and potions are one picture recoloured: on grey, an Iron Ore's picture scores 0.998 where a Silver Ore lies. Two held kinds found at one place with shape scores within `SAME_SHAPE` (0.02): the one nearer in colour is kept (`_recoloured`). Items the map's detector doesn't hold but whose pictures are recolours of a held one (`twins_of`, kept in a `twins/` subfolder) are weighed too: a find is dropped where a twin's colours are nearer.

**Text tests.** `FULL_MESSAGE` matches "You can't get anymore items." (seen when her Etc tab filled) and the usual wordings; `NO_DARTS_MESSAGE` matches the usual "no stars" wordings, since the game's own line has never been captured.

modules.title: Drop tables (what each monster drops)
modules.tagline: Which items to look for on a map, from meowdb's community drop lists.
modules.summary: A small data module: each known monster's Etc and Use drops, its reported mesos range and OSMLib's reference drop rates, read from meowdb's MapleStory Classic pages on 2026-10-24. `items_for(map)` tells the loot detector which item names to look for on a map (its monsters' drops plus four potions), with the first map pinned to what was seen there.
modules.details_md:
`MONSTERS` maps a monster's in-game name to a `MonsterDrops`:
- `items`: the community list's Etc and Use items with more up-votes than down-votes, leaving out scrolls (three pictures each, a shop pays 1), quest items (they drop only for a player on the quest) and arrows (a thief throws stars);
- `mesos`: the lowest and highest reported (None for a Red Snail; the Slime's from the first map, seen in game);
- `rates`: OSMLib's reference rates, used by the simulator's drops (`sim.world.game_drops`) and to weigh what a kill's pile is worth before a look sees it (`behavior.looting.expected_worth`).

Seven monsters are known: Horny Mushroom, Green Mushroom and Slime (Tree Dungeon), Stump, Dark Stump, Axe Stump and Red Snail (West Rocky Mountain II).

`items_for(model)` returns `PINNED`'s list for the first map (Victoria Road: Thicket Around the Beach II, `FIRST_MAP` 10000012: `FIRST_ITEMS`, what was seen where her kills died, plus potions); otherwise every drop of each known monster on the map in spawn order, then `POTIONS` (Red, Orange, White, Blue). `unknown` / `unknown_note` name the monsters with no entry, so the hunter and `watch` say so as they start instead of quietly looking for fewer drops. `safe` refuses item kinds Windows can't use as file names (a kind is also its picture's file name: "Omok Piece: Slime" would become an alternate data stream of a file "omok-piece").

The live stack uses the item names (what the loot detector looks for), the mesos ranges (what a bronze or gold coin is worth on a map: `behavior.looting.coins_for`) and the rates as weights only. The rates disagree with live play (her slimes' piles held Squishy Liquid 65% of the time on the first map, where OSMLib gives 40%).

modules.title: Death watch (DeathWatch)
modules.tagline: Sees a followed monster die by matching the game's die1 frames at its feet.
modules.summary: The game never says which monster died, and the monster detector has no die1 pictures, so a dying monster's track used to linger hidden for seconds. DeathWatch matches the game data's die1 animation frames around the feet of tracks that were found weakly or lost in the last 0.6 s; a match tells the tracker that monster is dying, about a second after the killing key. It watches only Tree Dungeon's Horny and Green Mushrooms, the kinds whose margins were measured.
modules.details_md:
**Why.** Her EXP rises about 0.2 s after the killing key (the server's), but the monster is still drawn alive and walking until her star lands, 0.85-0.9 s after the key; then it stops and plays die1 (a mushroom: 4 frames of 180, 180, 180 and 300 ms: eyes shut, sinking into its cap, the cap with a sliver of face, the cap alone fading) and is gone about 0.7 s later. Live, the service judged such a track dead a median 1.40 s after die1 began. The watch says which monster really died, so a kill bound to the wrong monster is put right and the throws after it stop, and another player's kill is dead at once instead of after `tracking.HIDE_S` (3.5 s). It comes too late for her next throw, which is decided about 0.45 s after the key from her EXP gain.

**How.** `DeathWatch.of(names_by_id, scale)` reads the die1 frames of the `MEASURED` kinds from the game data in memory (`gamedata.canvas.mob_frames`, about 0.5 s, nothing written) and draws them both ways at the look's scale (`pictures_of`: at 1366x768 only alpha-255 pixels count). Each frame `worldstate.WorldStep._dying` asks about tracks where `wants(score, since)` holds: detected in this frame under `REFOUND_UNDER` (0.9), or lost `RECENT_S` (0.6 s) ago or less, each track at most every `EVERY_S`. `best` matches every die1 picture in one window `PAD` px around the feet (8 masked matches in one C call, `match.best_matches`). `dying` fires on die1/1-3 at `DIE_GOOD` (0.7), or die1/0 (eyes shut, which looks like standing) at `DIE0_GOOD` (0.6) only for a track not found in this frame, and only if no other watched kind's die1 matches better there (`others`). (worldstate also takes deaths from `perception.exact`'s die1 finds, `_died_seen`, before asking the watch.)

**Measured.** On 16.8 minutes of recordings with 166 deaths labelled by eye, 118 of the 142 deaths on a track were seen (83%), a median 0.14 s after die1 began, and the 7 fires on no labelled death were all real deaths. Replayed in the service's frame step: 83 deaths seen, 73 of the 111 labelled and the other 10 real by eye. 0.83 ms a look on one thread.

modules.title: Spawn watch (SpawnWatch): newborns fading in
modules.tagline: Finds monsters fading in at spawn points by fitting an alpha blend over the map's art.
modules.summary: A monster the map spawns fades in over 0.817 s, and the colour-based whole-screen search only passes it at alpha 0.6-0.8, a median 7 frames (468 ms) late. SpawnWatch looks at every spawn point in view on every frame and fits the game's alpha blend of the kind's first pictures over the map's own art there; a fit that explains nearly all the difference is a newborn. On Tree Dungeon's clips it found 229 of the 233 newborns whose start shows (a median at their first visible frame, at alpha 0.065) with no false positive, then follows each until the whole screen finds it.
modules.details_md:
**The physics.** A newborn is drawn as F = B + a A (S - B): the map's art B behind it, its picture S with its own alpha A, and one opacity a over the whole picture, rising linearly at `FADE_PER_S` (1.224 a second). Its feet are on the spawn point (within 2 units across), in its move/0 picture (194 of 206 births) or stand/0, walking from the start.

**Onset at each point** (`SpawnWatch.look`, step 2). For every point whose window is in the play area (partly past the screen's top, left or right edge is fine; under the chat box or the game's windows it isn't: `ONSET_COVERED` False), with no newborn followed within `NEAR_POINT`:
1. *Empty test*: fewer than `EMPTY_COUNT` (20) pixels more than `EMPTY_LEVELS` (3) off the art: nothing there.
2. *The fit*: hypotheses are the `ONSET` pictures, both facings, feet within `BAND` (4) units of the point along its platform and `ROWS` (-1, 0, 1), every `STRIDE`-th (3rd) pixel of each picture. With D = F - B and G = A (S - B): a = D.G / G.G, R2 = (D.G)^2 / (G.G D.D), residual = sqrt((D.D - (D.G)^2 / G.G) / n), n the pixels kept times their 3 channels; the sums are integers with alpha 0-255, so the code's a is 255 D.G / G.G. The hypothesis explaining the most energy with `A_LO` <= a <= `A_HI` and `MIN_USED` of its pixels left is kept (`kept`); it is a newborn when a >= `A_MIN` (0.02), 1 - R2 <= `U_MAX` (0.008), residual <= `RES_MAX` (1.5 levels) (`passes`) and a <= `A_START` (0.8).
Her box (`HER_BOX`), the boxes of the monsters found the frame before (`MOB_BOX`), and art pixels that aren't the fixed art (animated objects: `Art.known`) are left out of the fit.

**Following** (step 1, `_follow`). Each newborn is looked for in every stand, move and hit1 picture, its feet up to `FOLLOW_SPEED` (180 units/s) times the time since it was last found ahead and `BACK` (3) behind, its alpha no more than `DROP_A` (0.08) under its highest (fainter means fading out). It ends when the whole screen finds a monster of its kind within `HANDOVER_DX`/`HANDOVER_DY` of it (`handed`), when the best fit is solid (a > `A_HI`), when it fits only fainter than `DROP_A` under its most (fading out: its place isn't looked at again until that fade is over), or after `LOST_AFTER` (2) unfound frames. A sighting becomes a `Mob` with `fading` set (`Sighting.mob`), so the tracker knows when it turns solid.

**Why the map's art, not a learned background.** A running median of the point came within 3.9 times of the rule as she walked past, and plates kept from unchanged windows gave a false positive; the art is never fooled by her standing on a point and needs no warm-up. It comes from `localization.mapart`, which the camera registration holds anyway.

**Cost.** The sums are integers (alpha 0-255, colours as they are), done in `gamelab/spawns.c` (8 hypotheses one column apart in AVX2 lanes) with the same integers as numpy: 1.19 ms a frame at the median, 1.7 ms more per newborn followed (numpy: 13.6 ms). It only runs at the game's own 1366x768 (a map unit a pixel), with the view registered on the frame, on `MEASURED` maps (Tree Dungeon).

modules.title: Touch watch (TouchWatch): her MISS and damage popups
modules.tagline: Reads the violet popup over her head: a monster touched her, MISS or damage.
modules.summary: When a monster touches her the game draws a violet popup above her name tag: MISS (her evasion took it) or the damage she took. TouchWatch finds violet text lines around her tag every frame, follows them, decides which were born on her, reads them against the game's own popup sprites, and waits up to 0.8 s for her HP bar to confirm a number. Each confirmed touch is a `Touch`; the module also defines INVULNERABLE_S, the 1.45 s after a touch when she can't be touched again.
modules.details_md:
**Before it.** A hit was her HP bar dropping and nothing else: every MISS, about half her touches for a high-evasion thief, went unseen.

**Violet lines** (`lines`). Two HSV ranges: `CORE` (hue 120-142, the popup's blue-violet top) and `ALL` (hue 118-165, the whole violet-magenta fill). Her own orange damage numbers and the pink-red criticals don't pass. The mask is closed, split into connected pieces, pieces merged into lines (gap up to `MERGE_GAP` 14 px), and a line is kept with at least `MIN_CORE` (80) blue-violet px, `MIN_SHARE` (0.25) of its violet, a height of 18-48 and a width up to 120 game px. Only a box around her tag is searched (`ROI`: 170 px either side, 260 above, 25 below).

**Whose** (`_look`). A line within `MATCH_DX`/`MATCH_DY` (plus 40 and `MATCH_VY` px a second: the camera eases) of a popup seen in the last `LOST_S` (0.45 s) is that popup. A new line is hers if centred within `BIRTH_DX` (26) of her tag with its bottom `BIRTH_DY` (165 to 55 px) above the tag's middle (`BIRTH_DY_PLACED` when the tag is hidden and placed by the camera); a little off (`EDGE_DX`, `EDGE_DY`) it is hers once it has lasted `EDGE_FRAMES` (3). A popup of hers born within `REFRACT_S` (1 s) of one already told, near it, is that one found again after her own numbers hid it.

**What it says** (`Reader`). The game's NoViolet0 small digits and Miss and NoViolet1 big digits (Effect.wz BasicEff.img), read from the game data copy as the watch is made (0.4 s), are turned into fill masks and matched with `TM_CCOEFF_NORMED`: MISS at 0.55 or more and 70 px wide or more; digits at a mean of 0.45 or more, 1-3 glyphs. Without the game data it goes by width (`MISS_W` 80: MISS is 98 wide, three digits 56-69).

**Confirming** (`update`, `_born_hers`). A MISS is told in the frame it shows. A number is held for her HP bar: a change over `HP_EPS` within `HP_WAIT_S` (0.8 s) makes it a DAMAGE touch (none of 135 damage touches had none); no change means another player's damage drawn over her, or a skill's flash, kept in `others`.

**Measured.** On 28.6 minutes of hunting (273 touches by eye): 269 found, none false, MISS or damage right on 268. 0.42 ms a frame at the median; the reader 4.7 ms on a touch's first frame. A MISS is told in its first frame; damage a median 0.04 s later (when her bar moves). Constants are in game px (1366x768); the watch scales them by `scale`.

**Around it, in worldstate.** An HP drop with no popup of hers told within `TOUCH_SAME_S` (1 s) is a touch too (`how` HP), and a MISS told off its popup followed by an HP drop within `HP_WAIT_S` becomes damage (a 'touch_fix' event): a damage number half hidden under her own orange numbers can be read as MISS by its width.

modules.title: Her attack's MISS (MissReader)
modules.tagline: Finds the orange MISS popup over a monster her attack missed.
modules.summary: When her star misses a monster the game draws MISS over it in the same red-to-yellow fill as her damage numbers. MissReader finds that word's shape in small boxes above her presses' targets by the overlap (IoU) of the fill's pixels with the picture's fill; 0.6 or more is a MISS. The key check (behavior.keycheck) counts a press followed by a MISS over its target as a key that worked.
modules.details_md:
The picture is the game's own Effect.wz BasicEff.img NoRed0/Miss (98x38, its origin at the bottom centre), cut into `gamelab/assets/misses/NoRed0_Miss.png` by `cut_assets`. Colour alone can't tell it: her damage numbers share the fill, and so do Tree Dungeon's orange platform undersides and maple leaves. The shape does. The picture's own mask is its opaque (alpha over 200), saturated (120 and up) fill pixels.

- `fill_mask`: OpenCV hue 27 or less, or 175 or more (red wraps), saturation 110 and value 190 or more (slack for JPEG and the start of the fade).
- `best`: the frame's fill mask is correlated with the picture's fill mask (`cv2.matchTemplate` `TM_CCORR`: the count of pixels both have at every place), the frame's own count under the picture's box comes from a box filter, and IoU = both / (picture + frame - both). The best place's IoU and its bottom centre (the picture's origin) are returned. A box with fewer fill pixels than `MISS_OK` times the picture's is skipped at once.
- `find`: pads each box by `SLACK` (6 px: the popup drifts up about 30 px a second and the camera eases) and keeps at most one MISS a box.

Measured on 26,968 saved frames (about 37 minutes of hunting): 5 MISS popups in 4 places, each read in 2-8 frames at 0.73-0.96; nothing else scored over 0.55. Drawn at 100, 80 and 60% opacity it reads 0.94, 0.80 and 0.24: only a popup's first half second reads. About 0.12 ms a box (README). Another player's MISS is the same picture: keycheck counts one only over her press's target, in its time. The violet MISS over her (a monster touching her) is another set, read by perception.touches.

modules.title: The game's words: message bar and pickup log rows
modules.tagline: Reads the game's own pink line above the HUD; picks the pickup log's OCR rows.
modules.summary: `ChatReader` reads the message bar (the chat's one line above the HUD), where the game says why it refused a key. The game's own lines are pink, so pink pixels tell a game line in under a millisecond and only a new one is OCR'd. `refusal` classifies a line as 'rope' (she's on a rope or ladder) or 'refused' (not enough MP). `log_rows` keeps the pickup log's OCR rows and drops the party window's names.
modules.details_md:
**Why it exists.** On 2026-10-26 she hung at the top of a rope on Tree Dungeon (on the rope, about 30 units under the platform her dot snapped her onto) and every Lucky Seven press was refused with "That cannot be used while you're on a rope or ladder." Her MP stayed put, and the out-of-darts watch stopped the hunt three times that night with her stars in her bag. Reading the refusal tells "the game refused the key" apart from "no stars left".

**The bar** is at game px x 290-830, y 703-727 of the 1366x768 window (`CHAT`, kept as fractions of the window so it scales; at 1920x1080 it's computed only, never seen). It shows the last chat line of anyone (the game's lines, notices, megaphones, chat), and a line doesn't fade: it stays until the next one replaces it. The game's own lines are pink (median RGB 244-248, 174-176, 185-188 on all 177 read off saved frames): `game_text` keeps red 200 or more, red - green 40 or more, red - blue 30 or more, and blue not under green - 5. Fewer than `MIN_TEXT` (40) pink pixels means no game line. `ChatReader.read` OCRs the bar (maplehelper.ocr's shared RapidOCR engine, about 285 ms) only when the pink pixels differ from the last read's (`ChatLine.same`: overlap of at least `SAME_SHARE` 0.9 of their union); otherwise it reuses the text. So the same refusal twice in a row can't be told from one left up.

**Refusals** (`refusal`). None for a line naming stars or darts (`loot.says_no_darts`: that's the game saying she has none, not a refusal), 'rope' for `ON_ROPE`, 'refused' for `REFUSED` (not enough MP to use a skill). "You are lacking the MP Potion that your pet is supposed to use." is neither.

**The pickup log** (`log_rows`). Its lines are right-aligned against the window's right edge, stacking up from y 606-616; the party window sits over it and its names stop short of the edge (the leader's star read as "7", a snowflake as a CJK sign). Rows not reaching within `LOG_RIGHT` (10/1366 of the width) of the edge are dropped.

`warm()` loads the OCR models on a thread of their own at a hunt's start (1.3 s), so the first read doesn't stall the hunt's own thread.

modules.tagline: Tells whether the chat box is expanded, collapsed or typing, from its +/- button.
modules.summary: An expanded chat box covers the bottom-left of the play area, hiding monsters there and her name plate. `read(frame)` tells EXPANDED, COLLAPSED or UNKNOWN from the box's 12x12 +/- button, its input row's white field and its navy 'All' tab (never its text), and whether its input line may have the keyboard (`typing`). behavior.chatcheck uses it to collapse the box at a hunt's start.
modules.details_md:
Read only on a whole frame of the 1366x768 client (`FRAME`): at other sizes the HUD is drawn scaled and no frame of it was kept, so the answer is UNKNOWN with `readable` False.

1. `glyph`: the button at (818, 709), 12x12 of the game's UI. Its border must be dark (at least `BORDER_LEAST` 36 of its 40 px no brighter than 48), its inside's white px must match the `MINUS` or `PLUS` mask within `GLYPH_OFF` (3) px, and at least `BLUE_SHARE` (0.9) of the rest must be blue. Minus means expanded (clicking it collapses), plus means collapsed. Because the glyph says what clicking does, it holds whatever the box's height, its lines' colours or what's over its upper part (a party invite, a megaphone's backing).
2. Plus: COLLAPSED, with `typing` if the field is white anyway (the input line open without the box: never seen, assumed).
3. Minus: also needs the field (x 372-808, y 707-724) white over `FIELD_SHARE` (0.75) and the 'All' tab navy over `TAB_SHARE` (0.6); else UNKNOWN. `marks` counts the field's non-white px; `TYPED_LEAST` (2) or more means text or a caret: `typing`.

Measured on two recordings (3,615 and 4,507 frames): 515 of 515 expanded frames and 7,606 of 7,607 collapsed ones read right (the one UNKNOWN: the mouse pointer over the button); no false EXPANDED on 107 saved shots and 3,077 Lie Detector frames. 0.04-0.08 ms a frame. The mouse pointer over the field marks it too, which is why behavior.chatcheck moves the mouse off the box once before believing either.

modules.title: Lie Detector spotter (LieDetectorSpotter)
modules.tagline: Recognises every form of the Lie Detector test so the hunt stops at once.
modules.summary: LieDetectorSpotter scores a frame against templates of each Lie Detector form: the countdown window's yellow title, the mouse mini-game's notice and board, the image quiz's warning and the quiz, and the Truth Booth (its clock and the Maple Administrator's name tag together). The elevated key player's watchdog calls it 4 times a second; a form at or over its threshold raises the alarm, which stops every plan. It also reads the Truth Booth's time left and tells which forms cover the play area.
modules.details_md:
**Forms.** Scores are each form's match as a fraction of its threshold; 1 or more means seen.
- *countdown*: a window titled "LIE DETECTOR" whose title bar is see-through, so the yellow letter shapes are matched, not raw pixels (`yellow`: red over 180, green over 140, blue under 110, red over blue by more than 110), at `THRESHOLD` 0.6;
- *`HALF_SIZE`* grey templates matched on the frame at half size: the mini-game's notice (0.9), the mini-game's board (0.8), the quiz's warning (0.7), the quiz (0.7) and the Truth Booth's clock (0.85). The notice comes 10 s before the board and the warning 30 s before the quiz, so the hunt stops and she retreats before the test begins;
- *truth booth*: the lesser of its clock and the Administrator's name tag (`BOOTH_TAG`, 0.8), because the clock alone is any timed map's.

**Frame sizes.** The templates were cut at 1920x1080. Since 2026-10-23 the game runs at its own 1366x768, where they scored only 0.32-0.64 of their thresholds, so such a frame is stretched to 1920x1080 first (`_stretched`), as the game itself used to stretch its view. A client of any other size is brought to 1920x1080 by its callers with `to_template` (shrunk by area or stretched with Lanczos: the watchdog, perception.frames).

**Where to look.** Each form has always shown at one place, the same pixel on every recording (`PLACES`). `near` matches each form only within `NEAR_MARGIN` (48) px of its places (11 ms of CPU at 1366x768); `scores` matches the whole frame (151 ms). The watchdog uses `near` and every `WHOLE_EVERY` (8)th look `scores`, so a form shown anywhere else is seen within 2 s; it uses `scores` every look during a cycle, on other sizes, and when the capture anchors are off (the game drawing its picture off its client moves every form off its places).

**Clock.** `clock_left` reads the booth's "Time Left": four digit slots (`CLOCK_SLOTS`), cream dots matched against `assets/clock_digits.png` at `CLOCK_MATCH` (0.8); a slot with under `CLOCK_INK` dots is blank. The watchdog uses it so a stay already seen isn't taken for a new one.

**Over the play area.** `over_play` names the form whose window lies over the play area (the countdown's window, the mini-game's board, the quiz), as `near` matches it: localization.locate counts her place "covered" under it; control.lie_tracking uses 'mini-game' and control.violetta_live 'countdown' to know when their game is up.

**Memory.** Each thread keeps its stretched, halved and grey scratch pictures (`_kept`): fresh ones were 8 MB a look at 1366x768 and 2,000 page faults that Windows' kernel zeroes.

The elevated key player imports this module, so it imports only gamelab.paths (tests/test_architecture.py checks what the player loads).

modules.title: Mini-game target tracker (TargetTracker)
modules.tagline: Follows the Lie Detector mini-game's fading, spinning figure by its outline.
modules.summary: In the Lie Detector's mouse mini-game a white figure fades to an embossed rim like the decoys printed on the board, then moves about 95 px a second while spinning at 2 rad/s over a scrolling board. TargetTracker takes the figure's outline as a template while it's white, then runs a 2,000-particle filter on edge-orientation evidence, a decoy check, optical flow off the board's scroll and a must-move rule. It answers where the target is each frame; it moves nothing itself.
modules.details_md:
**Template.** `target_blob` finds the white target among white blobs of 800+ px: pure white (core over 245) with a tan rim (B - R under -30; a countdown digit's rim is bluish). `template_from` takes the outline of its mask grown by `RIM` (8 px, the embossed rim that stays once the fill fades), sampled every `STEP` (3) px with each point's normal angle. The tracker restarts on every bigger white blob before START (4.6 s after the board's first frame).

**Evidence per frame.**
- *Outline* (`features`): Sobel gradients, the strong ones (above the 70th percentile) binned into `NB` (8) orientations over 180 degrees; for each template bin a response map by a table of bin distance (`LUT`), spread over `SPREAD` (3) px with one grey dilation (LINE-2D style). A pose's score is its points' mean response at the angle the spin predicts (`SPIN` 2 rad/s); a point off the board counts as the frame's typical score (`typical`: the median over a 32 px grid), neither a hit nor a miss.
- *Decoy check* (`LAM` 0.3): the same outline at the same angle where the board's scroll puts the pose `BACK_S` (0.2 s) earlier; a printed decoy rides the board, the target moves on its own.
- *Flow* (`MU` 1.0): DIS optical flow (medium preset) minus the board's scroll (`flow_shift`: the flow's median over the board's own pixels), the green cursor masked, averaged along the rim.
- *Must move*: a particle moving with the board loses weight (`GAMMA` 3, falling off over `SIG_REL` 50 px/s).

**Filter** (`_filter`). `N` = 2000 particles (x, y, vx, vy, angle offset). Each frame `TURN` (10%) of them, `TURN_EDGE` (30%) within `EDGE_PX` (70) of an edge, take a new direction at the target's usual speed (`TURN_V` 95 px/s) pointing away from a near edge, so a turn is followed in a frame or two. Weights are multiplied by exp(KAPPA (s + MU flow - LAM d)) and the must-move factor; systematic resampling when the effective count falls under N/2. The answer is the weighted mean of the particles within 40 px of the heaviest one.

**Speed.** 30 ms a frame on the 11 recorded rounds (92 before the speed work), against the 66 ms a frame of 15 a second: edge features by table and one dilation, the template turned once per distinct 2-degree angle, and the work spread over a pool as big as OpenCV's thread count beside the optical flow, particles scored in `PARTICLE_RUNS` (3) chunks.

**Accuracy.** Against reference tracks the user approved on all 11 recorded rounds: 3.5 px off on average, 97% of frames within 10 px, none lost.

Live, control.lie_tracking runs it in a child process at below-normal priority on the perception service's frames while the alarm is up, writes each answer to lab/lie_target/<time>.jsonl and hands the target's client position to the elevated player's cursor. `python -m gamelab lie-target` runs it on recorded clips and scores it (`track_clip`, `against_reference`).

modules.title: Violetta game solver
modules.tagline: YOLO boxes plus the client's shuffle rules: where the made-up Violetta ends up.
modules.summary: In the Lie Detector's Violetta game four Violettas are shuffled over four rounds and the player must pick the one wearing make-up. A YOLO11n model finds the Violettas (and the made-up one's face before the shuffles) in each frame; each round is solved by fitting the client's own shuffle animation, taken from its decompile, to the boxes over every start time, duration and permutation. It also spots the answer window (the buttons lit cyan) and the pass dialog's OK button.
modules.details_md:
**Detection** (`Detector`). Loads `assets/violetta.pt` (YOLO11n through ultralytics and torch, on the GPU if there is one) on first use and runs it on the stage crop (`CROP`: x 465-905, y 285-515 of the 1366x768 client) at `IMGSZ` 448 and `CONF` 0.5. The model was trained only on frames rendered from the game's own pictures (the stage, the sprites, the spotlights blended as the game blends them). Class 0 is a Violetta, class 1 the made-up one showing its face before the shuffles. A box's `size` is its width over `SIZE_W` (75.7 px at size 1.0).

**Before the shuffles.** `slots_of` measures the four slots' x (defaults `SLOTS` 526, 628, 730, 834) from frames with four boxes standing near them; `start_slot` votes the class-1 boxes, by score, into slots.

**The round's model** (the client's decompile, 2026-11-03). A round's motion lasts D in `DS` (3.8-5.0 s: 5000 - (rand % 5) x 300 ms), all four together, in one hop or two (each D/2). A hop of length T is a lift over T/4 to its lane's size, a straight travel over T/2 and a settle over T/4. The lane (drawn size, %) depends on direction and distance (`lane`): one slot left goes in front (116.5), one right behind (82.5), two or more right in front (152.5), two or more left behind (56.5); one that stays lunges in front (140) or behind (70).

**Solving** (`solve_round`). For each candidate start t0 and duration D, `_predict` gives every one of the 24 permutations' predicted x and log-size on every frame; `_support` sums, per prediction, its best box's Gaussian weight (`SX` 16 px, `SL` 0.14 in log-size). The best one-hop permutation is compared with the best chain of two hops, which must beat it by `TWO_MARGIN` (1.03) since two hops fit more. With the answer window's time known, t0 is pinned to window - D - `ROUND_END_S` (0.333 s) within `T0_SLACK` (0.4 s) and only frames from `LOOK_BACK_S` before are scored (round 1 had taken 218 frames and 20 s to solve). The answer is the server's: the client only animates it.

**The UI.** `buttons_lit`: the button row lit cyan over `BUTTONS_LIT` (30%) of its pixels means the answer window is open. `BUTTON_AT` gives the four buttons' middles. `OkDialog`: the pass dialog's template at `OK_AT` within `OK_NEAR` px, at `OK_MATCH` (0.8) or more, returns the OK button's middle.

Offline on the 9 recorded games of 2026-10-26 to 11-03: the made-up one's start slot on all of them and every answered round's slot as answered (28 of 28), though the model never trained on a real frame. control.violetta_live runs it live and clicks through the elevated player.

flows.title: How every monster on screen is found each frame
flows.summary: The perception service's pass searches the whole play area for monsters on every frame, on a thread beside her look; colour silhouettes pick places, masked picture matches confirm them.
flows.trigger: Every frame of the perception service's pass (localization.worldstate.WorldStep.step, 15 a second).

steps.text: At the game's own 1366x768, with the real detector, submits `detect_wide` on the full frame to the pass's one-thread pool 'wide' before her look (then perception.exact's finder on the same thread); otherwise `Eyes.monsters_wide` runs after the look.
Cuts the rows above the HUD into bands of WIDE_BAND every WIDE_STEP, overlapping by the tallest learned picture, and searches them at once on the bands pool.
Each band is shrunk (area-averaged, in C) to SEARCH_SCALE and cut to a multiple of COARSE.
In search.c: each unit's colour test, silhouettes scored where the cover test keeps a window, peaks at SILHOUETTE_THRESHOLD, then places; shapes OpenCV's noise could decide are redone its way.
Each place passes the gate at step 1's scale if one of its first pictures scores FINE_GATE (0.55).
Each passing place's best FINE_TEMPLATES pictures are matched at full size FINE_SLACK px around, in native.c; THRESHOLD (0.6) or more becomes a Mob with its feet from the picture's origin (`_seen`).
Overlaps suppressed across bands; a find of a twin kind (Axe Stump vs Stump) re-judged at its feet by `_pick_kind`.

The pass waits for the search's answer (the spawn watch ran meanwhile); newborns it hasn't found are added (`_handed`) and so are the exact finder's finds (`_exact_added`); all are placed on the map and go to the tracker (localization.tracking) to be matched to tracks.

flows.summary: The spawn watch fits the game's alpha blend at every spawn point in view, follows each newborn while it fades in, and hands it to the whole screen's detections once the search sees it.
flows.trigger: Every frame with her placed and the view registered on it, on Tree Dungeon at 1366x768 (worldstate.SPAWNS).

steps.text: Passes the frame, the view's top-left, the time, her feet and the feet of the monsters the tracker matched in the frame before (not fading, not the exact finder's) to the watch; on a frame it can't use (her not placed, no sure view, a bad frame), `missed()`.
First re-fits each newborn already followed (`_follow`): ok, solid, fading out, or a miss (LOST_AFTER 2).
For each point, its window's pixels in the play area; points partly under the chat box or game windows are skipped; off-screen parts are filled with the art.
The empty test: fewer than EMPTY_COUNT pixels off the art by more than EMPTY_LEVELS means nothing there.
Integer sums D.G, G.G, D.D per hypothesis (ONSET pictures, both facings, BAND and ROWS around the point), in spawns.c or numpy, with her box and other monsters' boxes masked.
`scores` gives alpha, R2 and residual; `kept` picks the best hypothesis; a >= A_MIN, 1 - R2 <= U_MAX, residual <= RES_MAX and a <= A_START make an onset Sighting and a newborn to follow.
`SpawnWatch.handed` drops newborns the whole screen found too (same kind within HANDOVER_DX/DY); the rest become Mobs with `fading` (Sighting.mob) beside the search's detections.
The tracker follows the newborn as any monster, and uses FADE_PER_S to know when it turns solid.

flows.title: A violet popup over her becomes a touch
flows.summary: Each frame the touch watch finds violet lines around her name tag, decides which popup is newly hers, reads MISS or digits, and confirms a number by her HP bar.
flows.trigger: Every frame of the pass that passed its checks (worldstate.TOUCHES); new popups are looked for only with her tag known (seen or placed).

steps.text: Calls `TouchWatch.update` with the frame, her tag (seen or placed), whether it was seen, her HP bar share and the time.
Settles held numbers first: an HP change over HP_EPS makes a DAMAGE touch; none within HP_WAIT_S means another player's.
Finds violet text lines (CORE/ALL hue ranges) in the ROI around her tag.
Matches each line to a popup seen in the last LOST_S; a new one born within BIRTH_DX/BIRTH_DY of her tag is hers (or at the edge once it lasts EDGE_FRAMES).
Skips a popup already told within REFRACT_S; else `_classify` reads it with `Reader.read` (MISS or digits; by width without the sprites). MISS is told now; a number is held for her HP bar.
Each Touch becomes a 'touch' event and the state's newest touch ('crowded' if another player's dot is near and only the popup says so).

The stack reads it: a new touch (`Senses.touched_since`) cuts the navigator's chain short; `invulnerable_until` (INVULNERABLE_S after the popup, a 'crowded' one left out) lets a chain pass a monster while it lasts; the hunter logs it.

flows.title: A Lie Detector seen: from the watchdog's look to the alarm and the helpers
flows.summary: The elevated key player's watchdog checks the screen 4 times a second; a form seen raises the alarm, and the perception service's helpers follow the mini-game's target or the Violetta game while it's up.
flows.trigger: The key player's 'lie-detector-watch' thread, every 0.25 s (control.player.Watchdog).

steps.text: On a 1366x768 frame with a capture anchor in place, asks the spotter's `near`; every WHOLE_EVERY-th look, during a cycle, or at another size, `scores` of the whole frame.
Stretches the frame to 1920x1080, halves and greys it, matches each form's template within NEAR_MARGIN of its PLACES; the Truth Booth is the lesser of its clock and the Administrator's tag.

A form at 1 or more: the watchdog sets its alarm event first (keys stop within about 10 ms), then `raise_alarm` writes lab/ALARM.json and a screenshot and pages by form; the player refuses every plan but the few kinds the alarm allows.
In the Truth Booth, the clock's seconds left are read so a stay already seen isn't taken for a new one.
While the alarm is up the perception service asks `over_play` for 'mini-game'; the board's crops go to a child process.
The child process follows the target each frame; its client position goes to the elevated player's cursor and to lab/lie_target/*.jsonl.

For the countdown's Violetta game (`over_play` 'countdown'), each frame's boxes (violetta.Detector), the round solved at each answer window (`buttons_lit`, `solve_round`) and its button clicked through the player; the pass's OK by `OkDialog`.

not_done: The monster re-find code (MobDetector.refind, refind_all, refind_ahead, native.c's rf_* and the GPU path) has been unused by the live pass since 2026-10-30, left for a later cleanup.

Monsters partly covered near her (by her body, pet, name plate, numbers, effects) are mostly missed by the masked search: on a clip of 2026-11-02 it found a monster within 25 units of her on 6% of the frames, 700 of its 791 misses refused at FINE_GATE. Since 2026-11-04 perception.exact's finder (another slice) adds them; the masked match at a missed track's predicted box (the design's MISSED_CHECK) stays unbuilt.

The spawn watch's README notes (2026-11-01) say it had not yet run in game; other maps aren't measured, points under the chat box aren't looked at, and only 20 of 90 newborns whose start is hidden are found (every stand and move picture at the onset would find 12 more for about 3 times the cost).
The death watch only watches Tree Dungeon's Horny and Green Mushrooms; other kinds wait for a replayed recording to measure their margins.
Touches: 4 of 273 are lost (MISSes half under the Lie Detector's window or split by her own orange numbers, read as digits); a half-MISS template was deferred.
The game's message for having no throwing stars has never been captured: says_no_darts matches guessed wordings.
The chat box is read on every frame, but only at 1366x768, and acted on only at a hunt's start (behavior.chatcheck); an input line open with the box collapsed has never been seen (taken as typing).
Drops of monsters not in drops.MONSTERS aren't looked for (only potions and mesos).
The mini-game tracker's one real miss is a faint stretch where a same-shaped decoy sits 60 px away.
The Violetta model was trained only on rendered frames; it was checked offline on 9 recorded games.
Monsters and drops are looked for only above the HUD's top (row 700 at 1366x768): a monster half under the chat bar isn't looked for.
